Here's the whole thing, start to finish.

## What it is

Every animated surface on that board is the **same one engine** drawing into a different shape. There is no library of card components. There is a single WebGL fragment shader, and a "shape" number tells it whether to paint a disc, a sphere, a rounded rectangle (the trading card and the pill), or the wings. One shader, four masks. That is why the system feels coherent: the card, the icon and the hero are literally the same code, not four things built to look alike.

## The core idea (the ethos)

**A gradient is data, not a picture.** A core is four colours, each with a position and a weight, plus one dark shading colour. That is the whole thing. Once a core is described that way, it stops being a 200KB image you have to ship and becomes four hex values you can put in a JSON file. New gradient means a one-line edit, and every treatment updates at once.

The visual philosophy underneath it is **"one chassis, many cores."** The geometry, the light and the mark never change. Only the colour moves. So the system's honesty test is section 03 of the board: same disc, same shading, same wings, swap only the gradient. If it holds there, it holds everywhere.

Two craft details do most of the work:
- **Colour is mixed in linear space, not sRGB.** Mixing raw sRGB goes muddy grey through the middle, which is why most gradients look cheap. This one converts to linear, mixes, converts back.
- **The colours drift on mismatched orbits and are sampled through a warped coordinate.** That warp is what makes it churn like liquid instead of just rotating.

## How a gradient gets ingested

This is the part you rebuild with any new gradient. A Python script (`build.py`) does it once, offline:

1. Downsample the source gradient PNG to 160×160.
2. Run **k-means (k=5)** over the pixels with a **fixed seed**. Five colour clusters fall out.
3. The **darkest** cluster becomes the shading colour.
4. The **other four** become the moving anchors. Crucially, each anchor keeps *where* it lived in the source (a colour that was top-right stays top-right) and *how much* of the image it was (an accent stays a small accent instead of averaging away).
5. Write those numbers out.

The fixed seed matters more than it looks: it means two rebuilds produce identical palettes, so you can compare gradients without them shifting under you. That is the entire ingestion system. Point it at a new PNG, get a new core.

## The files

```
build.py                    the ingestion + generator (Python)
orb-template.html           hand-edited source · one orb
expressions-template.html   hand-edited source · the whole board
palettes.json               the extracted colour data
  ↓ run build.py
index.html                  GENERATED · the board you're looking at
orbs/<ID>.html              GENERATED · standalone orbs
```

The one rule: **you only ever edit the two `*-template.html` files.** Everything else is generated and gets overwritten. Want to change how every core looks? Edit the template, rerun the script. Want to fix one gradient's colours by hand? Edit `palettes.json`, rerun. Never touch `index.html` directly, your changes vanish on the next build.

## The one clever bit of engineering

The board has 53 live surfaces. The obvious way (one WebGL canvas each) breaks, because browsers only allow about 16 and silently kill the rest. So instead there is **one** offscreen WebGL context. It renders a surface, then copies that image into that surface's own cheap 2D canvas. Every card shares a single GPU engine and just takes a stamp of it. That is the trick that lets 53 fluid gradients run on one page without melting the machine.

## How to rebuild it with a new gradient

Drop your new gradient PNG in the source folder, add its ID to the list, run `python3 build.py`. The script extracts the palette, and every treatment (disc, sphere, card, pill, favicon) renders in the new colour automatically. No shader edits, no new components.

The one honest caveat: this **approximates** the source gradient, it doesn't reproduce it pixel-for-pixel. You're trading exactness for the core becoming four editable numbers. If you ever need an exact match to the Figma swatch, use the flat static image instead.
